subcategory: critically endangered native perennial wild rice

planting.note: Only obtain plants or rhizome divisions from a permitted conservation propagation program, never from wild collection; establish divisions in flowing, spring-fed water held at a stable 68-72F year-round, anchoring the base in gravelly substrate where current keeps the long ribbon-like leaves streaming just below the surface.

directions: Texas wild rice survives naturally only in the upper stretch of the San Marcos River in Hays County, Texas, where constant-temperature spring flow lets it grow as a true perennial instead of the annual habit of its northern relatives Zizania aquatica and Zizania palustris. It anchors itself in flowing water over gravel or sand, sending up long, ribbon-thin submersed leaves that stream downstream while a separate flowering culm reaches above the surface to set seed. Listed as federally endangered since 1978 because of reduced spring discharge, recreational trampling, and competition from non-native aquatic vegetation, it should never be collected from the wild; conservation nurseries propagate it by division for reintroduction and research plantings. Its dense underwater foliage stabilizes streambed sediment and shelters the endangered fountain darter and San Marcos salamander, making it a keystone species of one of the most biologically unique spring ecosystems in North America.
sources: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service Species Profile: Texas Wild-Rice
Texas Parks & Wildlife Department Listed Species Program
Texas State University Meadows Center for Water and the Environment

planting.note: Press corms into saturated mud or shallow water up to about 12 inches deep as soon as the site thaws in spring; this is the most cold-tolerant of the arrowheads, so it can be planted earlier than southern Sagittaria species.

directions: Arum-leaf arrowhead ranges farther north than any other North American Sagittaria, growing wild in shallow ponds, marsh edges, and slow streams from Alaska and the Yukon south through the Rocky Mountains and Great Lakes to New Mexico. It is smaller and daintier than broadleaf arrowhead, with narrower, more triangular leaf blades that taper to a rounded arum-like base rather than the sharp basal lobes typical of the genus. The starchy corms, known as wapato, were an essential root vegetable for many Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest and northern Plains, traditionally gathered by wading barefoot through the mud to loosen corms so they floated free. Its extreme cold tolerance and ability to persist under ice make it a good choice for northern water gardens, and the corms and foliage provide food for waterfowl, muskrats, and beaver.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Guide: Wapato (Sagittaria cuneata)
USDA Forest Service Celebrating Wildflowers Plant of the Week
University of Michigan-Dearborn Native American Ethnobotany Database

planting.note: Set rhizome divisions in spring into saturated mud or shallow water at lake, pond, or freshwater tidal shore margins; unlike bolder arrowheads it tolerates some wave and current action once established.

directions: Sessile-fruited arrowhead departs from the classic arrowhead look of its relatives, producing narrow, lobeless, lance-shaped leaves instead of the sagittate blades that give the genus its common name. It occurs naturally in lakes, ponds, and fresh-to-slightly-brackish tidal river shores from the Canadian Maritimes and upper Midwest south to the mid-Atlantic, Tennessee, and the Ozarks. The plant produces small white, three-petaled flowers followed by rounded seed heads that sit directly against the stem without individual stalks, a feature that gives the species its name and distinguishes it from every other native arrowhead in the field. Grown in a pond margin or bog garden, it adds a fine-textured, grassy foil to the coarser foliage of broadleaf and lanceleaf arrowheads while offering the same habitat value to marsh birds, amphibians, and aquatic invertebrates.
sources: Native Plant Trust Go Botany: Sagittaria rigida
Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in standing water up to about a foot deep or in permanently saturated soil in full sun; confine to a large lined pond or aquatic basket, as this species spreads vigorously by rhizome and can quickly dominate small water features.

directions: Typha orientalis is the dominant native cattail of Australia, New Zealand, and much of eastern Asia, forming tall, dense stands along the coastal lowland lakes, slow rivers, and lagoons of the Southern Hemisphere in the same ecological role that Typha latifolia fills in North America. It sends up broad, strap-shaped leaves and stout stems topped with the familiar brown, sausage-like flower spike, growing considerably taller than most cultivated cattails. Known as raupo to the Maori and cumbungi in Australia, its rhizomes and young shoots have a long history as a traditional food source, roasted or pounded into a starchy meal. Because it spreads rapidly by rhizome and self-seeds readily, it is best reserved for large constructed wetlands, treatment ponds, or restoration plantings where its exceptional capacity for sediment trapping and nutrient uptake can be put to use rather than in small ornamental water gardens.
sources: Florabase, Western Australian Herbarium: Typha orientalis
New Zealand Plant Conservation Network: Typha orientalis

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring as a marginal in up to about a foot of standing water, or in permanently moist bog soil at a pond edge; the creeping rhizomes spread readily, so allow room or plant in a sunken container to control its reach.

directions: Sweet galingale is a temperate sedge native to marshes, ditches, and pond margins across southern Europe, North Africa, and western Asia, and it is considerably more cold-hardy than the tropical papyrus relatives more commonly grown in water gardens. Slender triangular stems carry loose, glossy umbels of golden-brown flower clusters in late summer above a dense clump of grass-like foliage. Its creeping yellow rhizomes are pleasantly aromatic and were candied as a sweetmeat and distilled for perfume oil in medieval Europe, where the plant was traded as 'English galingale,' a fragrant, spicy-scented alternative to true tropical galangal. In the modern water garden it is valued as a hardy, fine-textured marginal for pond edges and rain garden basins, spreading by rhizome to knit together wet banks while offering shelter to amphibians and aquatic invertebrates.
sources: Plants For A Future (PFAF) Database: Cyperus longus
Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland (BSBI)

planting.note: Set divisions after all danger of frost has passed and water has warmed, with crowns a few inches below the surface in rich aquatic soil; in climates outside its hardiness range, overwinter potted specimens indoors in a heated greenhouse or bright frost-free space.

directions: Aztec pickerelweed is a larger, distinctly tropical counterpart to the familiar North American pickerelweed, native to freshwater marshes and pond margins from Mexico and Central America south to eastern and southern Brazil. Its lance-to-heart-shaped leaves rise on petioles that can stretch nearly a yard long, well above dense spikes that can carry fifty or more violet-blue flowers through the warm season. Unlike Pontederia cordata, it carries no frost tolerance and dies back completely if water freezes, so gardeners outside the tropics grow it as a container marginal that gets moved to a frost-free spot for winter. Where it does thrive outdoors year-round, it offers a bold, oversized architectural presence at pond edges and draws bees, skippers, and other pollinators to its long summer-to-fall bloom.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online (POWO): Pontederia sagittata
